answers.implementation_then_now: The protection answer is the lowest option on both dates, so implementation is Does Not Apply in 2023 and 2026. No documented practice of a grace period for job seekers was found for either period. Nothing in the window changed the rule tying worker categories to the employer, or the cancellation ground in art. 129(1).
answers.sourcing_note: The SINALEVI consolidated texts (current versions) show per-article amendment notes. Arts. 80, 96 and 129 of Ley 8764 carry no amendment note at all. Arts. 108 and 113 of the Reglamento were last amended by Decreto 42389 (Jan. 2022), before the window, and art. 109 carries no note. The 1 Jan 2023 text is therefore reconstructed as identical. The full art. 289 text was only partly visible.

answers.starting_answer_concern: As the first coder notes, cancellation is not literally automatic. Art. 289 of the Reglamento requires a reasoned resolution following the Title VII procedure, and art. 96 allows a change of category. Some reviewers might prefer the middle option, but there is no 'specified time period', so the 0 option is defensible.
answers.notes: No change in the window. Non-work statuses (permanent residence, family-based residence, refugees) are unaffected by job loss on both dates. Ley 10645 (Feb. 2025) amended art. 94(4) on students and teachers, not worker categories.

answers.implementation_then_now: No source was found that documents how DGME actually handles temporary-to-permanent changes, for either period. The starting answer's figures come from DGME 2021 statistics reported in the press (El Observador, not reopened here). They predate the window but are the closest thing to evidence for the 2023 date. The OECD International Migration Outlook 2025 describes 2024–2025 procedural changes, such as filing temporary-residence applications from abroad through a power of attorney, aimed at speeding up immigration processing. That is policy, not documented outcomes. No report of the art. 78(1) route being refused as a policy was found for either date, so 'Usually' is kept for both, with low confidence.

(Así reformado por el artículo 28 de la Ley ... N° 10437 del 29 de enero de 2024)

answers.implementation_then_now: For 2023, the US State Department 2023 Country Report finds the Ministry of Labor enforced wage, overtime and safety laws effectively around San José. Enforcement was weaker in rural areas 'particularly where large numbers of migrants were employed'. The report also notes too few inspectors, no power for inspectors to fine, and back-pay processes 'habitually subject to lengthy delays'. Agricultural migrants hired on short contracts through intermediaries were more vulnerable. The 2024 report repeats the same findings almost word for word. Nothing documents a shift, so 'Sometimes; Usually' holds on both dates. These sources cover migrant workers generally, mostly agricultural, and do not single out irregular workers.
